newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's 13 pct lead boosts Democrats in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's 13 pct lead boosts Democrats in Congress.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's lead over Republican Bob Dole is hovering above 13 percent, a lucky number for Democrats seeking to resume control of Congress, Reuters' tracking poll showed on Monday.

Clinton pulled 46.8 percent of likely voters in the poll, compared with 33.6 percent who picked Dole and 7.3 percent who chose Reform Party candidate Ross Perot; 2.4 percent listed "other" as their choice and 9.9 percent were undecided.
The 13.2 percent gap between Dole and Clinton was significant because of the so-called 13 percent rule, according to Reuters' pollster John Zogby.

"Once Clinton's lead gets up to 13 percent, the Democrats have more of a shot at taking the House of Representatives; he has a coattail effect," Zogby said in a telephone interview. "If Clinton's lead goes under 13 percent or sinks into single digits, you see the Republicans swing back."

Acknowledging that support for Clinton had been relatively shallow, Zogby said his wide margin still had the potential to help congressional Democratic candidates. Asked which party's candidate they would choose for Congress if the election were held now, poll respondents picked Democrats over Republicans, 39.2 percent to 35 percent.

One reason for Clinton's surge, Zogby said, was an abortive foray by Dole's camp to persuade Perot to bow out of the race and throw his support to Dole. The resulting publicity brought Perot back to centre stage less than two weeks before the Nov. 5 election.
"To say that Bob Dole hurt himself last week with the overture to Ross Perot is putting it mildly," Zogby said.

In addition to depressing Dole's poll numbers while boosting Clinton's, the attempt to sideline Perot actually appears to have helped the independent candidate, whose numbers now approach 8 percent after being stuck at around 5 percent for weeks.
Monday's Reuters tracking poll surveyed approximately 1,000 likely voters over a three-day period that began on Friday and ended on Sunday. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.
